title: deep-review silently ignores its args: docs pass a string, the script reads an object
description:
Observed live on 2026-08-02 during a human-requested deep review of TASK-181 and TASK-175. Both runs silently discarded their arguments and reviewed the wrong thing by default. This is the same silent-success class as TASK-181's `ok:true` defect and TASK-184's stale operator doc — a control that reports success while not doing what was asked.

**The contradiction.**
- `skills/orchestrator-routing/SKILL.md:963` (and the `.claude/skills/` parity copy) documents the invocation as a CLI-style string: `/deep-review base=<git-ref> ticket=<TASK-key>`. Line 948 repeats the same shape in prose.
- `workflows/deep-review.js:80` and `:89` read `args.base` and `args.ticket` — i.e. they require `args` to be an OBJECT.

Passing the documented string form (`args: "base=bc585e3 ticket=TASK-181"`) leaves `args.base` and `args.ticket` `undefined`.

**Why it is silent.** The guard validates arg CONTENT but never arg SHAPE:

```js
let baseRef = 'origin/main';
if (args && args.base) { ... else log('[warn] args.base ... falling back') }
let ticketKey = null;
if (args && args.ticket) { ... else log('[warn] args.ticket ... dropping ticket context') }
```

Both `[warn]` branches sit INSIDE `if (args && args.<field>)`, so they fire only when a field is present but invalid. A `args` that is a string, a malformed object, or missing the fields entirely takes neither branch and produces no warning at all. The run proceeds against `origin/main` with `ticketKey = null` and logs a cheerful `Deep review starting — base: origin/main`.

**Observed consequence.** Two runs were launched with explicit `base=` and `ticket=`. Both reviewed `origin/main...HEAD` with no ticket anchor. The AC-compliance dimension fell back to its no-ticket prompt (`No ticket key was supplied`) and audited for generic incomplete-implementation smells instead of auditing the diff against the ticket's actual acceptance criteria — which is the single dimension most directly aimed at "did we build what was asked". The second run, intended to anchor on TASK-175, became a duplicate of the first.

Coverage survived only by coincidence: `origin/main` happened to equal the requested base (`bc585e3`). Had HEAD been pushed first, both runs would have reviewed an empty or near-empty diff and reported findings against nothing, with no signal that anything was wrong.

**Fix direction (decide, do not assume).** Two independent problems, and BOTH need fixing — correcting only the docs leaves the silent-degradation path intact for the next malformed call:
1. Make the documented invocation and the accepted arg shape agree. Decide which is canonical — accept the documented `key=value` string form by parsing it, or change the docs (both parity copies) to the object form — and make the other conform.
2. Fail loudly on an unusable `args`. A deep review that cannot honour its requested base or ticket must say so prominently, not proceed on defaults. Consider refusing to run at all when `args` is present but unparseable, since a silently-redirected review is worse than no review — the human believes a gate ran.

Note for whoever picks this up: `workflows/deep-research.js` may share the arg-shape convention; check it for the same defect rather than fixing this one in isolation.
acceptance_criteria: A failing spec first reproduces the defect: invoking the workflow's arg-handling with the DOCUMENTED string form ('base=<ref> ticket=<KEY>') currently yields baseRef 'origin/main' and ticketKey null, with no warning emitted. Capture the red-run output verbatim as the tests-first evidence.

The documented invocation and the accepted arg shape agree. Decide which is canonical and record the decision in the closing comment; whichever is chosen, skills/orchestrator-routing/SKILL.md and its .claude/skills/ parity copy are updated byte-identically, and the workflow accepts what the docs describe.

An unusable args value (a string when an object is expected, a malformed object, or fields present but unparseable) no longer degrades silently: it emits a prominent warning naming what was ignored, or refuses to run. Decide which — a silently-redirected review is worse than no review, since the human believes a gate ran.

The shape guard is covered by specs for each distinct bad input: args as a string, args as null/undefined, args as an object with unknown keys, and args with a present-but-invalid base or ticket (the existing [warn] paths must keep working — they are correct today and must not regress).
workflows/deep-research.js is checked for the same arg-shape convention and either fixed in the same pass or explicitly cleared, with the finding recorded in the closing comment.

An end-to-end check proves a ticket-anchored run actually anchors: with a valid ticket arg, the AC-compliance dimension receives the ticket's acceptance criteria rather than the no-ticket fallback prompt.
npm run test:all is green; no existing workflow spec regresses; if any bundled source changed, dist rebuilt via npm run build:plugin and committed with dist-parity passing.

comments.author: orchestrator
comments.body:
CLOSED on a green re-review after one fix round. **APPROVE — 0 HIGH / 0 MEDIUM / 0 LOW.** All 7 ACs PASS.

**Review depths:** first pass `full` (486 changed lines; the multi-agent review machinery other reviews run on). Fix round `light` — **rubric-derived, not an override**: 89 changed lines across 3 files, under the 150 threshold, touching no mandatory-FULL surface (workflow scripts are not bundled into `dist/` — `bin/init.js` copies `workflows/` from disk at runtime — and `workflows/` is not `src/`), with the same file already having had a full-depth pass at `0d40fd1`. The reviewer retained one-way escalation and reported that nothing triggered it.

## AC2 DECISION (the AC requires this recorded here): the STRING form is canonical
The ticket framed this as a docs-vs-code contradiction where either side might be authoritative. That framing was half wrong, and the developer adjudicated it correctly: **the docs were never wrong — only the script was.** No documentation changed; `skills/orchestrator-routing/SKILL.md:963` and `:948` were already correct, and both parity copies stayed byte-identical.

The reviewer verified this independently on three lines of evidence: (a) `workflows/deep-research.js:44-52`, the sibling workflow under the same runtime, has always validated `args` as a raw string and works in production; (b) every documentation surface describes the slash-command string form and nothing anywhere ever documented an object invocation; (c) the live incident is dispositive — the runs were launched with the string form and `args.base`/`args.ticket` read `undefined`, which is only possible if the runtime delivered a string.

## AC5 DECISION (also required here): deep-research CLEARED, not fixed
`workflows/deep-research.js:44-52` already refuses `typeof args !== 'string' || args.trim().length === 0` with an `[error]` log and an error-shaped return. Verified independently by the reviewer. No fix needed — it is the precedent the refuse path now follows, not a second instance of the defect.

## AC3 decision: refuse vs warn, split by severity
A wholly unusable `args` (wrong type, or a non-empty string with zero recognizable tokens) **refuses to run**: `refuse()` returns before any `pipeline`/`agent` call, emitting `{ confirmed: [], summary: { refused: true, reason, blocked: true } }`. A string carrying some recognized fields plus noise **warns**, naming exactly what was ignored, and proceeds. Per-field invalid values keep the pre-existing warn-and-fallback.

**The refuse path genuinely dispatches nothing** — proven in the specs with throwing stubs, and re-verified by the reviewer literally.

## The fix round — why this did not close on the first APPROVE
The first review returned APPROVE with one MEDIUM, and I sent it back rather than closing, because the MEDIUM was **a residual instance of the exact class this ticket exists to close**: `base= ticket=TASK-181` — a present-but-empty value — ran against `origin/main` with no warning and no refusal. The key parsed so the refuse path never fired, and `''` is falsy so `if (parsed.base)` skipped both anchoring and the warn branch. Realistic shape: `/deep-review base=$REF` with an empty shell interpolation reproduces the original incident's consequence exactly — the human believes the gate ran against their ref.

Closing a silent-degradation ticket with a silent degradation inside it is not a close.

**Fixed at `ceb334c`** by changing the presence check from truthiness to key presence (`'base' in parsed`), so `''` falls through into the existing `GIT_REF_RE`/`TICKET_KEY_RE` validation and lands in the pre-existing warn branch — no new code path invented. Literal outcome verified by the reviewer outside the spec harness: `[warn] args.base "" failed the git-ref allowlist — falling back to 'origin/main'`, with the valid sibling ticket still anchoring.

Also fixed: `refuse()` now sets `blocked: true`. A review that never ran must not read as non-blocking to a consumer checking only `summary.blocked`. A repo-wide grep confirmed no consumer depended on the old `false`.

## Evidence quality — both reviewers re-derived rather than trusted
The first reviewer ported all 11 spec assertions into a scratchpad harness and ran them against the pre-fix file pulled from git, reproducing exactly 8 failures / 3 passes rather than accepting the claimed red run. The fix-round reviewer killed all three new specs by mutation (reverting `'base' in parsed` to truthiness, and `blocked: true` to `false`), confirming none is vacuous — and noted that the start-line assertion alone would have survived the first mutant, so the warn assertion is the real discriminator.

## Gate
Fix round: `test:since -- ceb334c~1` 1 file / 14 passed (non-zero selection) · `npm test` 79 files / 1069 passed, 2 skipped · three named e2e specs 23 passed · parity byte-identical · no dist exposure (no bundle embeds the workflow body; confirmed by grep across all 8 bundles).

## Carried forward, not blocking
Duplicate keys silently last-win (`"base=a base=b"` yields `b` with no warning) — cosmetic, deliberately left. And a parallel-run flake was observed in `tests/workflows-deep-review-args.spec.js` during full-suite runs by a different reviewer: the spec evals the live workflow file at runtime, so it is sensitive to concurrent edits. It passes 14/14 in isolation and green on re-run. Worth tracking if it recurs.

**Process note for my own record:** neither reviewer was given the developer's hand-off, so both re-derived the red-run evidence from scratch. That is my briefing gap, not a developer omission — the evidence existed. Forwarding hand-off artifacts to reviewers is now standard practice.
